method: four independent extractions; every regex cross-tested against the pooled negative examples of all four. tier1 = compiles, fires on its own positives, fires on zero pooled negatives, author confidence high.

tier1.name: not-just-x-its-y
positive_examples: It's not just a cache, it's a consistency boundary.
This isn't just a latency problem — it's a correctness problem.
It's not just a caching problem - it's a correctness problem.
This isn't just about latency, it's about trust.
It's not merely a config change, it's a contract change.
negative_examples: The regression is not just in the write path; the read path also slowed.
It is not only slower, it fails closed on timeout.
The p99 regression is not in the serializer but in the codec.
The p99 did not just rise; it rose 40x, from 30 ms to 1.2 s.
We are not replacing the codec but wrapping it.
The budget is not about fairness; it is 3 attempts over 250 ms.
tier1.repair: Drop the negated half and assert the claim once: 'The cache is the consistency boundary.' If both halves carry information, they are two sentences with two subjects, not one elevation move.
tier1.source_quote: _it's not just X, it's Y_
tier1.detection_note: The load-bearing element is the doubled copula: the same dummy subject ('it'/'this'/'that' + is) on both sides of the pivot. Legitimate 'not just A but also B' constructions carry a real subject on at least one side, which is why both negatives stay silent. Verified against both.

tier1.name: goblin-token
positive_examples: There are a few goblins hiding in the retry path.
We inherited some goblins from the v1 scheduler.
negative_examples: The `goblin_mode` flag is disabled in production.
We ripped out the gremlin script that randomly killed pods.
tier1.repair: Name the actual defect: 'three unguarded retries', 'an unbounded queue'. The word carries no technical content and marks the sentence as generated.
tier1.source_quote: _[goblins](https://openai.com/index/where-the-goblins-came-from/)_
tier1.detection_note: Lookarounds exclude identifier contexts, so `goblin_mode` and GOBLIN_MODE-style code spans do not fire (verified). Run after stripping fenced/backticked code, like every lexical rule here. The only genuine over-fire domain is a document actually about game content, which the target genres are not.

tier1.name: creature-in-metaphor-frame
tier1.regex: \b(?:like|as if it(?:'s| is| were)|is basically|is essentially|think of .{0,28}? as|imagine|picture)\s+(?:a |an |some |the |your |our )?(?:little |tiny |angry |friendly |grumpy |mischievous |hungry |sleepy |grouchy )?(?:goblin|gremlin|ogre|raccoon|imp|sprite|elf|elves|dragon|wizard|monster|critter|creature|troll|frog|pigeon|gnome)s?\b
positive_examples: Think of the GC as a raccoon rummaging through the heap.
The retry storm is basically a troll under the bridge.
Imagine a tiny frog hopping between shards.
negative_examples: The frog-boiling failure mode is well documented in the SRE book.
Pigeonhole principle guarantees at least one bucket holds two keys.
Internet trolls generate a disproportionate share of abuse reports.
Think of the cache as a bounded queue with an eviction policy.
tier1.repair: Drop the creature and state the comparison in mechanism terms: what resource does the analogue consume, what does it contend with, what is its rate.
tier1.source_quote: most uses of frog turned out to be legitimate
tier1.detection_note: This encodes the source's own auditing lesson: the same lexeme is a tic or legitimate depending on frame, so the rule is frame-gated rather than lexeme-gated. Requires an explicit simile/metaphor frame immediately before the creature noun, which is why troll/frog/pigeon can be included here but not in the bare lexical rule. Zero corpus false positives. Known miss: a creature introduced as a bare subject ("The gnome that owns the lock table") has no frame and will not fire.

tier1.name: clipped-negative-fragments
positive_examples: No prior. No nostalgia.
No config. No daemons. No excuses.
negative_examples: No configuration file is required for the agent.
No retries are issued after the budget is exhausted; the request fails fast.
tier1.repair: Merge the fragments into one sentence that says what is absent and why it matters: "The agent reads no config file; every knob is a flag."
tier1.detection_note: Requires two consecutive verbless "No X." sentences, which is what distinguishes the rhythm from a single legitimate negative statement. Recovered from the version history, which added "clipped negative endings" in 2.5.0 and folded them into pattern 2 in 3.0.0.
tier1.source_quote: Added deeper-truth claims, announcements, repeated headings, and clipped negative endings.

tier1.name: pause-command
tier1.regex: (?:^|[.!?]\s+)(?:wait|pause|stop|think about (?:it|that)|let that sink in|read that again)\.
positive_examples: Let that sink in.
Wait. The lock was already held.
negative_examples: Wait for the canary to bake for 30 minutes.
The client must wait until the lease expires.
tier1.repair: Delete the command. If the next fact is the surprising one, put the surprise in the fact: "The lock was already held by the same thread - the mutex is not reentrant."
tier1.detection_note: The imperative must be the whole sentence, which is what separates it from "wait for"/"must wait". From the 2.11.3 note, folded into pattern 2 in 3.0.0.
tier1.source_quote: Added decorative arrows to §18 and pause commands and one-word shouting to §31.

tier1.name: deepity-opener
tier1.regex: \bat its core\b|\bat the end of the day\b|\bwhen all is said and done\b|\bthe (?:true|real) (?:essence|nature) of\b|\bis the language of\b
positive_examples: At its core, what matters is trust.
At the end of the day, latency is a product decision.
negative_examples: At the core of the scheduler sits a min-heap.
The essence of the algorithm is a two-pass scan over the WAL.
tier1.repair: Cut the opener and keep the claim, then make the claim specific enough to be wrong: "Users abandon the page after 2 s, so p95 is the budget that matters."
tier1.detection_note: "at the core of X" (a real component) is legitimate and is excluded by requiring the possessive "its". Aphorisms of the form "X is the language of Y" are caught only in that exact shape; other coined maxims need a human read.
tier1.source_quote: **Sayings that sound deep** | "At its core, what matters is...", "Symmetry is the language of trust"

tier1.name: staged-run-up
tier1.regex: \blet'?s (?:dive|jump) (?:in|into)\b|\bbefore we (?:dive|jump|get started)\b|\bwithout further ado\b|\bbuckle up\b|\bhere'?s the (?:thing|kicker)\b|\blet'?s (?:unpack|break it down)\b|\bstrap in\b
positive_examples: Let's dive into the flame graph.
Here's the thing: the lock is fair.
negative_examples: Let's walk through the timeline minute by minute.
Before we deploy, the canary must hold for 30 minutes.
tier1.repair: Delete the run-up and open on the first fact: "The flame graph puts 61% of CPU in the codec's copy loop."
tier1.detection_note: "Let's walk through" and "before we deploy" are ordinary and useful in postmortems and runbooks, so the verb list is restricted to dive/jump/unpack/break-it-down. "The thing is," was deliberately excluded - engineers write it in correct prose.
tier1.source_quote: **Staged run-up before the point** | "Let's dive in", "Honestly? It depends..."

tier1.name: borrowed-authority
positive_examples: Experts believe the approach scales.
It is widely accepted that tail latency dominates.
negative_examples: Dean and Barroso show that tail latency dominates at scale [2013].
Research shows the same effect (https://example.com/report).
The benchmark shows a 3x regression on the write path.
tier1.repair: Name the source and what it measured, or delete the claim: "Dean and Barroso (2013) measured a 10x tail amplification at 100 fan-out."
tier1.detection_note: The negative lookahead suppresses the rule when a citation, link, DOI, or "et al." follows within the same sentence, so a properly sourced claim never fires. Singular "the benchmark shows" / "the profile shows" are excluded - those name a specific artifact.
tier1.source_quote: **Borrowed authority** | "Experts believe...", "cited in NYT, BBC, FT, and The Hindu"

tier1.name: decorative-heading
positive_examples: ## 🚀 Launch Phase
## Strategic Negotiations And Partnerships
### Deploy → Verify → Rollback
negative_examples: ## Why the retry budget ran out
## HTTP/2 Flow Control
### Rollback plan
## Retry Budget Exhaustion
tier1.repair: Sentence case, no emoji, no arrows: "## Deploy, verify, rollback".
tier1.detection_note: Two alternatives. The emoji/arrow branch is exact. The title-case branch needs four or more consecutive Capitalized-lowercase words, which is why "HTTP/2 Flow Control" (acronym breaks the run) and "Retry Budget Exhaustion" (only three) do not fire, while a four-word title-case heading does. The `(?-i:...)` scope is required so the branch still works under a case-insensitive compile - without it this rule fires on every heading.
tier1.source_quote: **Decorative headings** | "Strategic Negotiations And Partnerships", "🚀 Launch Phase:"

tier1.name: chatbot-residue
tier1.regex: \b(?:great question|certainly[!,]|i hope this helps|hope that helps|let me know if you(?:'d| would) like|feel free to ask|as an ai|i'?m happy to help|here'?s a (?:comprehensive|detailed) (?:overview|breakdown|guide))\b
positive_examples: Great question! The scheduler is preemptive.
Let me know if you'd like me to expand the rollback section.
negative_examples: Let me know if the repro steps are unclear.
Ask in #perf-oncall if the dashboard is empty.
Certainly not: the lease is not renewed after a fence.
tier1.repair: Delete the wrapper sentence and keep the content.
tier1.detection_note: "Let me know if..." is only flagged in the "you'd like" offer form, which keeps the legitimate reviewer-facing version in the first negative example. "In conclusion," and "To summarize," were deliberately left out: a summary paragraph in a long RFC legitimately opens that way. "Certainly" requires the following punctuation so the adverbial use does not fire.
tier1.source_quote: **Chatbot residue** | "Great question! ... I hope this helps!"

tier1.name: hype-announcement
tier1.regex: \b(?:big news|exciting (?:news|update|announcement)|we'?re thrilled to|we'?re excited to (?:announce|share)|happy to announce|drum ?roll)\b
positive_examples: Exciting news: the new codec is live!
We're thrilled to announce v2.
negative_examples: v2 is live in prod01 as of 14:00 UTC.
Announcing the deprecation: v1 endpoints stop serving on 2026-10-01.
tier1.repair: Lead with the change, the environment, and the date: "v2 is the default in prod01 as of 2026-09-18."
tier1.detection_note: From the version history ("Expanded §28 to cover casual announcements"), folded into the staging patterns in 3.0.0. A plain "Announcing X" with a date is a legitimate release note and does not fire.
tier1.source_quote: Expanded §28 to cover casual announcements.

tier1.name: knowledge-limit-disclaimer
tier1.regex: \bas of my (?:last |knowledge )?(?:update|cutoff|training)\b|\bi (?:do not|don'?t) have access to\b|\bbased on (?:the )?available (?:information|sources|data)\b|\bwhile (?:specific )?details (?:are|remain) (?:limited|scarce|unclear)\b
positive_examples: As of my last update, the API supported v2.
Based on available information, the cluster was healthy.
negative_examples: We could not determine whether the LB or the client closed the connection; trace ids were not propagated.
Metrics cover only the last 7 days; the 30-day view was not retained.
The cause is unconfirmed: we have a correlation in time and no trace.
tier1.repair: Say what you checked, what it showed, and what is missing: "Access logs cover 14:00-15:00 only; the connection-close side is not recoverable from them."
tier1.detection_note: Honest uncertainty is mandatory in postmortems and must never fire - all three negative examples state precisely what is unknown and why, which is the correct form. Only the model-shaped disclaimers fire. "It appears that" was deliberately excluded from the regex: it is used both by a hedging model and by an engineer describing a genuine inference, and no regex separates them. Flag it only in a human or LLM pass, and only when the sentence names no evidence.
tier1.source_quote: **Knowledge-limit disclaimers and guesses** | "While details are limited in available sources, it appears..."

tier1.name: participial-significance-tail
positive_examples: The team moved the fleet to the new runtime in Q3, underscoring its commitment to reliability.
Tail latency fell 18 percent, highlighting the significance of the new cache tier.
The service was adopted by four orgs, cementing its role as the default ingest path.
negative_examples: We pinned the kernel version, reflecting what the hosts actually run.
The flame graph is annotated, highlighting the hot path in red.
The dashboard was regenerated, reflecting the new role assignments for on-call.
The retry budget was cut to two, reducing tail amplification by half.
tier1.repair: Delete the tail. The sentence before the comma already carries the fact; the participle adds an unsourced evaluation. If the significance is real, make it its own sentence with a measurement or a decision attached ('This is why we kept the cache tier after the Q4 cost review').
tier1.source_quote: This is often done by attaching a present participle ("-ing") phrase at the end of sentences, sometimes with vague attributions to third parties
tier1.detection_note: The abstract-noun requirement plus the following-preposition/punctuation anchor is what separates this from legitimate participial tails ('reflecting what the hosts run', 'highlighting the hot path in red'), which take concrete objects. A tail whose object is a measurement or a named component is fine and will not fire.

tier1.name: legacy-significance-phrase
positive_examples: The 2019 rewrite stands as a testament to the team's discipline.
The GA release marks a pivotal moment for the platform.
The move to columnar storage represents a fundamental shift in how we query.
negative_examples: The commit marks the boundary between the two schema versions.
The sentinel value serves as a guard against double free.
This represents a 12 percent shift in traffic to the new cluster.
The migration cemented the v2 schema in place for every caller.
tier1.repair: Say what changed and for whom. 'The GA release marks a pivotal moment' becomes 'After GA, the v1 write path is frozen; three teams must migrate by Q2.' If there is no such consequence, delete the sentence.
tier1.source_quote: Words to watch: stands/serves as , is a testament/reminder , a crucial/pivotal/vital/significant/key role/moment ... represents/marks a shift , key turning point
tier1.detection_note: Requires both the verb and the canned abstract complement. 'marks the boundary', 'serves as a guard', 'represents a 12 percent shift' are literal and will not fire, because the complement is concrete or numeric.

tier1.name: boasts-copula-avoidance
positive_examples: The new host boasts 8 H100 GPUs and 2 TB of RAM.
The cluster is home to the feature store and the ranking service.
negative_examples: The box has 8 H100 GPUs and 2 TB of RAM.
The boastful tone in the launch doc was cut before review.
The cluster hosts the feature store and the ranking service.
tier1.repair: Use 'has' or 'runs'. 'The host has 8 H100s'; 'The cluster runs the feature store and the ranking service.'
tier1.source_quote: LLMs prefer to use marketing -related verbs like features , offers , and the like to their neutral synonym has
tier1.detection_note: Deliberately narrow. The full copula-avoidance family in the source ('serves as', 'features', 'offers', 'functions as') cannot be linted, because 'the WAL serves as the durability boundary' and 'the sidecar functions as the TLS terminator' are ordinary correct engineering prose. Only 'boasts' and 'is home to' have essentially no legitimate technical use.

tier1.name: slop-vocabulary-core
positive_examples: We delve into the scheduler internals in the next section.
The config layer is a vibrant tapestry of per-tenant overrides.
The proposal garnered support from three orgs.
negative_examples: Attach Delve to the running binary with dlv attach.
We use dlv (Delve) for stepping through the goroutine.
The OIDC realm is configured per environment.
The benchmark harness is carefully calibrated against production traces.
tier1.repair: 'delve into' -> 'walks through' / 'covers'. 'garnered support' -> 'three orgs signed off'. 'tapestry', 'vibrant', 'multifaceted', 'treasure trove' -> cut entirely; they carry no information in a design doc.
tier1.source_quote: delve , [...] intricate/intricacies , [...] meticulous/meticulously , [...] tapestry (as an abstract noun), [...] vibrant
tier1.detection_note: Requires 'delve' to be followed by 'in/into' specifically, because Delve is the Go debugger and 'attach Delve to the binary' is a legitimate sentence. 'realm' likewise requires 'of', since OIDC/Kerberos realms are real nouns. I deliberately left out source-listed words that are load-bearing in engineering prose: key, crucial, robust, landscape, enhance, align with, intricate. Those need a per-document density count, not a per-occurrence fire.

tier1.name: vague-plural-authority
positive_examples: Industry reports suggest the pattern is common at this scale.
Experts argue that the sidecar model is the wrong default.
negative_examples: The Kafka docs note that rebalances are stop-the-world.
Two reviewers argued for the simpler design in the RFC thread.
Researchers at Google published the Borg paper in 2015.
The SRE report notes three separate saturation events.
tier1.repair: Name the source or delete the claim. 'Industry reports suggest' -> 'The 2025 Netflix post-mortem (link) reports the same pattern at 200k rps.' In a design doc an unattributable claim is a guess wearing a citation's clothes.
tier1.source_quote: AI chatbots tend to attribute opinions or claims to some vague authority—a practice called weasel wording . They also commonly exaggerate the quantity of sources
tier1.detection_note: Only unnamed plural authorities fire. 'Researchers' and 'scholars' are excluded because ML design docs routinely and correctly write 'Researchers at DeepMind showed...'; a named institution makes the attribution checkable. Named singular sources ('The Kafka docs note') never fire.

tier1.name: despite-these-challenges-closer
positive_examples: Despite these challenges, the service continues to serve as the system of record.
The platform faces several challenges as adoption grows.
negative_examples: Despite the retry budget, the request failed after three attempts.
We hit three specific problems: clock skew, GC pauses, and a bad DNS TTL.
Despite its size, the index fits in page cache.
The schema continues to be read by two legacy jobs.
tier1.repair: Enumerate the problems with owners and dates, then stop. Delete the reassuring closer entirely — 'Despite these challenges, X continues to thrive' is the sentence that tells a reader the section had nothing in it.
tier1.source_quote: Many LLM-generated Wikipedia articles include a "Challenges" section, which typically begins with a sentence like "Despite its [positive/promotional words], [article subject] faces challenges..." and ends with either a vaguely positive assessment
tier1.detection_note: The source is explicit that the tell is the formula, not the word 'challenge'. Vague-quantifier 'faces several/numerous challenges' fires; a concrete count with an enumeration ('faces three challenges: A, B, C') will still fire on 'several'-class words only, so a doc that says 'faces three challenges' is clean by construction. Reviewers should not report the 'faces several challenges' arm when a colon-delimited list follows within the same sentence.

tier1.name: canned-wrapup-heading
positive_examples: ## Key Takeaways
### Future Outlook
## Conclusion
negative_examples: ## Risks and Mitigations
## Background and Motivation
## Rollback Plan
## Decision
tier1.repair: Rename to the thing the section decides: 'Decision', 'Open questions', 'Rollout plan', 'Action items (owner, date)'. 'Key Takeaways' and 'Conclusion' almost always restate the body; delete the section and move any real content up.
tier1.source_quote: Section or subsection headers in the format of "X and Y" are common in (but not exclusive to) AI generated articles. [...] which may also include a separate section for "Future Prospects."
tier1.detection_note: Needs re.MULTILINE. I did NOT generalise the source's 'X and Y' heading rule, because 'Risks and Mitigations', 'Background and Motivation', 'Goals and Non-Goals' are standard RFC headings. Only the specific canned wrap-up titles are listed. 'Conclusion' is the softest member: some house RFC templates mandate it, so suppress it if the repo's template contains it.

tier1.name: in-conclusion-restate
positive_examples: In summary, the rollback restored p99 within four minutes.
Overall, the migration was net-positive for cost.
negative_examples: Overall throughput rose 12 percent after the change.
The summary table is in Appendix A.
We concluded the incident at 14:32 UTC.
The overall p99 budget is 250 ms.
tier1.repair: If the paragraph introduces no new fact, delete it. If it does, drop the connective and lead with the fact: 'The rollback restored p99 within four minutes.' Engineering readers scan; a restatement paragraph costs them a scan and returns nothing.
tier1.source_quote: When generating longer outputs (such as when told to "write an article"), older LLMs often added sections titled "Conclusion" or similar, and often ended paragraphs or sections by summarizing and restating its core idea.
tier1.detection_note: The required comma is what separates the connective from the adjective/adverb: 'Overall throughput rose 12 percent' and 'the overall p99 budget' do not fire. Report only when the flagged sentence opens the final paragraph of a section and contains no number or name absent from the section above — a lead paragraph that summarises up front is good writing, a trailing one is filler.

tier1.name: assistant-chatter
positive_examples: Certainly! Here is the breakdown of the retry budget.
Let me know if you'd like me to expand the rollback section.
negative_examples: Let me know if the repro steps are unclear.
Here is the call graph for the hot path.
Of course the leader can fail mid-commit; that is what the lease is for.
You are right that the timeout is wrong.
tier1.repair: Delete. This is chat-session residue that was pasted into the document; nothing in it is addressed to the document's reader.
tier1.source_quote: Words to watch: I hope this helps , Of course! , Certainly! , You're absolutely right! , Would you like... , is there anything else , let me know , more detailed breakdown , here is a ...
tier1.detection_note: Narrowed hard from the source's list. Bare 'let me know', 'here is a', and 'of course' are all normal in PR descriptions and doc bodies, so each is required to appear in its full canned form ('let me know if you'd like', 'Of course!' with the exclamation point). This is the highest-precision rule in the set and should be treated as blocking.

tier1.name: unfindable-source-hedge
positive_examples: As of my last knowledge update, the retention policy was seven days.
Specific details about the sharding scheme are limited.
The eviction policy is not widely documented.
negative_examples: The rebalance protocol is not documented in the client README.
We could not find the config in the repo; it is generated at build time.
The information in the trace is enough to rule out GC.
Details about the sharding scheme are in design doc DD-204.
tier1.repair: Say where you looked and what you would need. 'Not widely documented' -> 'Not in the service README or the 2024 design doc; asked @owner in #team-storage on 2026-09-14.' The vague form hides that nothing was checked, and it is usually followed by a fabricated guess.
tier1.source_quote: Words to watch: Up to my last training update , as of my last knowledge update , While specific details are limited/scarce... , not widely available/documented/disclosed , ...in the provided/available sources / search results...
tier1.detection_note: The adverb (widely/extensively/publicly/readily) is required. A located negative claim — 'not documented in the client README' — is falsifiable and does not fire. In engineering prose this rule usually catches the sentence immediately before a hallucinated mechanism, so flag the following sentence for a human read too.

tier1.name: unfilled-placeholder
positive_examples: Best regards, [Your Name]
url = PASTE_DASHBOARD_URL_HERE
access-date = 2025-XX-XX
negative_examples: See [the design doc](https://go/dd-204) for details.
The array index arr[i] is bounds-checked at the call site.
// TODO(spopuri): drop the v1 path after the migration
The window is [start, end) and end is exclusive.
tier1.repair: Fill it in or delete the surrounding claim. A shipped design doc containing [Insert benchmark numbers] is worse than one that says 'not measured yet, owner @x, due 2026-10-01'.
tier1.source_quote: AI chatbots may generate responses with fill-in-the-blank phrasal templates [...] However, some LLM users forget to fill in those blanks.
tier1.detection_note: Markdown links, array indexing, interval notation, and conventional in-code TODO comments are all explicitly excluded — a bare '// TODO(owner):' is legitimate engineering practice and must not fire. Only bracketed imperatives, SCREAMING_SNAKE paste tokens, and XX-dates fire.

tier1.name: emoji-heading
positive_examples: ## 🚀 Rollout Plan
### 🔍 Root Cause
negative_examples: ## Rollout Plan
| ✅ | canary | passed |
- ✅ Backfill complete
#### Root cause
tier1.repair: Delete the emoji. Heading text should be greppable and diffable; a rocket adds no information and breaks anchor links in some renderers.
tier1.source_quote: In particular, they sometimes decorated section headings or bullet points by placing emoji in front of them.
tier1.detection_note: Needs re.MULTILINE. Scoped to headings only. The source also lists emoji-decorated bullets, but status glyphs in tables and checklists (✅/❌/⚠️) are normal and useful in engineering docs, so bullets and table cells are deliberately excluded.

tier1.name: broader-landscape-tail
positive_examples: The change reflects a broader move toward declarative config.
This sits within the evolving observability landscape.
The rewrite is part of a broader trend in the industry.
negative_examples: This is part of a broader migration off Thrift.
The Kubernetes ecosystem has three competing CNI plugins.
We widened the scope to include the write path.
The context deadline propagates to every downstream call.
tier1.repair: Name the specific programme or delete the framing. 'part of a broader trend' -> 'the third of five services moving off Thrift under DD-118'. A trend the doc cannot name is a trend the author invented to make the change sound inevitable.
tier1.source_quote: LLM writing often puffs up the importance of the subject matter by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects of the topic represent or contribute to a broader topic.
tier1.detection_note: 'part of a broader migration off Thrift' names a concrete referent and does not fire; only the abstract nouns (landscape, ecosystem, narrative, movement, trend) do. 'ecosystem' and 'context' are common technical nouns and fire only when governed by broader/wider/evolving/changing/shifting.

tier2.name: assistant-turn-tic
positive_examples: You're absolutely right, the lock is held across the I/O.
I hear you on the rollback risk, but the config was already live.
negative_examples: The reviewer was right that the committed offsets were stale.
Confirm the shard assignment is right before you cut over.
tier2.repair: Delete the sentence. A design doc, RFC or postmortem has no conversational turn to acknowledge; if the point being conceded matters, state the point itself.
tier2.source_quote: _load-bearing_; _it's not just X, it's Y_; _you're absolutely right_; _I hear you_
tier2.detection_note: Verified: fires on both positives, silent on both negatives. The separator is the second-person pronoun immediately before 'right' - engineers write 'X was right', never 'you're right', in a document. Near-zero false-positive risk in the target genres because these are dialogue moves, not prose.

over_fires_on.sentence: You are right that the timeout is wrong.

tier2.demoted: fires on 1 negative example(s) from the pooled adversarial set

tier2.name: bare-predicative-load-bearing
positive_examples: This is load-bearing.
That assumption is actually load-bearing, so tread carefully.
negative_examples: The load-bearing assumption is that clocks are monotonic across the fleet.
The 10% retry budget is load-bearing for the availability math.
tier2.repair: Say what rests on it: 'the availability math assumes this retry budget'. The metaphor is only worth its space when the dependent is named.
tier2.source_quote: _load-bearing_
tier2.detection_note: A blanket ban on 'load-bearing' would catch careful engineers, so the regex targets only the bare predicative form with no stated dependent. Attributive use ('the load-bearing assumption is that...') and predicative use followed by for/because/on/in-that are excluded, and both negatives are verified silent. Downgraded from high because the narrowing is my inference; the source names the phrase without qualifying it.

tier2.name: reviewer-verdict-tic
positive_examples: The capacity reasoning here is hand-wavy.
Let me smoke-test that assumption before we commit to the migration.
negative_examples: I hand-wave the constant factor here; Appendix B has the bound.
The smoke test suite runs before the canary is promoted.
tier2.repair: For hand-wavy: state which step is unjustified. For smoke-test: say what you will actually run, or use 'check' - reserve smoke test for a test that executes.
tier2.source_quote: _hand-waving_; _smoke-test_
tier2.detection_note: Both words have legitimate engineering senses, which is the whole difficulty. The split that works: the verb 'hand-wave' (author declaring their own elision, legitimate) versus the adjective 'hand-wavy' (verdict on someone's reasoning, the tic); and 'smoke test' applied to a test suite (legitimate) versus applied to an idea/claim/assumption (the tic). Verified: both legitimate negatives stay silent.

tier2.name: nonce-suffix-coinage
positive_examples: The failure was rate-adjacent rather than a hard timeout.
That framing is very enterprise-coded.
negative_examples: The flush interval is hard-coded to 200ms.
The write-ahead log is fsynced before the ack.
tier2.repair: Replace with the relation you mean. 'Rate-adjacent' is either 'caused by rate limiting', 'correlated with request rate', or nothing at all - pick one.
tier2.source_quote: 1 in every 5 words is a novel compound word (ex: ‘rate-adjacent’) which itself is the model's invented stand-in for a metaconcept that i need to interrogate it about
tier2.detection_note: Scoped to four productive slop suffixes rather than hyphenation generally. '-shaped' was tested and dropped: 'U-shaped latency curve' and 'L-shaped tail' are legitimate. The hard-/soft-/base- lookahead is mandatory - without it 'hard-coded' fires and the rule is dead on arrival. Verified against both negatives.

tier2.name: stacked-negation-in-contrast
positive_examples: I am holding the logging branch to actionable-cause output, not merely non-JSON prettiness.
The rollback path is not simply unreliable; it is untested.
negative_examples: The write is not durable until fsync returns.
We do not enable the shim for non-LinkedIn traffic.
tier2.repair: Resolve the double negative into a positive claim: 'the log line must name the cause', not 'not merely non-JSON prettiness'. Then decide whether the contrast is needed at all.
tier2.source_quote: The action is buried beneath invented compound words, stretched metaphors, opaque contrasts, and double negatives.
tier2.detection_note: Restricted to the exact shape in the source's quoted Sol passage - a negated contrast whose second term is itself un-/non- prefixed - because the general 'two negations near each other' test fires on ordinary guard-clause prose ('if the queue is not empty and the worker is not draining'). Verified silent on both negatives. Recall is deliberately low; this catches the densest instances only.

tier2.name: ceremonial-filler
positive_examples: Let us delve into the scheduler's admission path.
The lease duration plays a crucial role in failover latency.
negative_examples: We lean on the scheduler for fairness rather than on client backoff.
We used Delve to attach to the running process.
tier2.repair: Delete, or replace with the measurement: 'lease duration sets the failover floor at 12s'. Every item here is deletable without information loss, which is what makes the rule safe.
tier2.source_quote: stretched metaphors
tier2.detection_note: Deliberately excludes items with a literal technical reading: 'at the end of the day' (batch jobs literally run then), 'north star' (a real dashboard name at many companies), 'double-click on' (literal in UI docs), 'at its core' (fine writing). 'delve into' is required as a bigram so the Go debugger Delve does not fire - verified. Each surviving item is pure filler, so a false positive still costs the author only a deletion. Medium rather than high: the source says 'stretched metaphors' without naming these.

positive_examples: The allocator gets grumpy once fragmentation passes 40 percent.
The database is having a bad day whenever the vacuum runs.

negative_examples: The scheduler decides which task runs next based on vruntime.

tier2.source_quote: You must undercut pretension through playful use of language.
tier2.detection_note: Mechanism-derived, not stated in the source: the reward was for a playful register, and the creature nouns were one surface of it. Emotional attribution to machinery is the same register reaching for a different part of speech, so it is a predicted tell this corpus has not logged. The adjective list deliberately excludes the anthropomorphisms engineers use correctly and constantly - wants, decides, waits, is confused, is unhappy, is angry - because those are load-bearing technical idiom and banning them would be the linter-ignoring failure mode. Restricted to whimsy-only moods.

tier2.name: mischief-as-root-cause
tier2.regex: \b(?:gremlins?|goblins?|gnomes?|gnomes|gargoyles?)\s+in the\s+\w+|\b(?:some|a|the)\s+(?:mischievous|naughty|cheeky|impish|devious little|gremlin-like)\s+\w+|\bwreak(?:ed|ing|s)? havoc\b|\bcame back to haunt\b|\bplaying hide[- ]and[- ]seek\b|\bdecided to misbehave\b|\bgot into mischief\b
positive_examples: There were gremlins in the pipeline that week.
Some mischievous interaction between the two retry layers wreaked havoc on the fleet.
The bug was playing hide-and-seek with our tracing.
negative_examples: A misbehaving client sent 400k requests per second to the control plane.
The killswitch exists so that a misbehaving rule can be disabled quickly.
The regression had been lurking for years before the test suite caught it.
tier2.repair: A postmortem that attributes a defect to mischief has no root cause in it. State the trigger, the mechanism, and the propagation path, or write "cause not yet identified" and file the follow-up.
tier2.source_quote: A few months later, the goblins came back to haunt us in a much more specific and reproducible form.
tier2.detection_note: Highest-value rule for postmortems specifically, because whimsical agency is a substitute for causal analysis. The naive version of this rule is unshippable: bare "misbehaving" and "lurking" fire five times legitimately in the corpus (Brooker on misbehaving clients, Cloudflare's killswitch, Gregg's misbehaving Ubuntu service, Dan Luu on latent bugs), so both are excluded and only the agentive form "decided to misbehave" survives.

tier2.name: wonder-adverb
positive_examples: The failure mode is delightfully weird: the cache serves stale entries only on Tuesdays.
A gloriously simple fix: bump the timeout.
negative_examples: This works beautifully if and only if the condition is based on truthiness.
Building a delightful ergonomic photo editing website is a different problem.
The behavior is strange: latency drops when we add load.
tier2.repair: Cut the adverb. If the finding is surprising, the surprise is in the data; "the cache serves stale entries only on Tuesdays" already carries it.
tier2.source_quote: The world is complex and strange, and its strangeness must be acknowledged, analyzed, and enjoyed.
tier2.detection_note: Derived from the rewarded system prompt quoted in the source: the Nerdy persona was instructed to enjoy strangeness, so the reward gradient favours delight-marking adverbs generally, not just creature nouns. "beautifully" is excluded because PEP 572 uses it correctly ("works beautifully if and only if") and "delightful" as a bare adjective is excluded because Brooker uses it correctly ("a delightful ergonomic photo editing website"); only the -ly wonder adverbs, which appear zero times in 50 engineering documents, are matched.

tier2.name: undercut-pretension-aside
tier2.regex: \bplot twist\b|\bspoiler(?: alert)?[:,]|\bhere'?s the (?:fun|best|wild|spicy|juicy) part\b|\(\s*yes,?\s*really\s*\)|\(\s*no,?\s*really\s*\)|\(\s*don'?t ask\s*\)|\bi know,? i know\b|\bfun fact[:,]
positive_examples: Plot twist: the config had been correct the whole time.
Here's the fun part: the failover target was the same host.
Fun fact: the retry budget was never wired up.
negative_examples: The twist in the plot of this incident is not relevant; here is the timeline.
The interesting part of the trace is the 40ms gap before the first read.
Note: the retry budget was never wired up.
tier2.repair: Delete the aside and keep the clause after the colon. "The failover target was the same host" is the finding; the wink adds nothing and costs the document its severity.
tier2.source_quote: You must undercut pretension through playful use of language. [...] Tackle weighty subjects without falling into the trap of self-seriousness.
tier2.detection_note: Directly grounded in the reward-bearing system prompt the source quotes. These are the narrated-reveal markers a model reaches for when rewarded to avoid self-seriousness. Zero corpus hits. Note that the semantically similar but sober forms - "Note:", "Of note:", "Unexpectedly," - are not matched and are the intended repair target.

tier2.name: reveal-framing
tier2.regex: \b(?:here|this|that|now)(?:'s| is| was) (?:where|when) (?:it|things|the fun|the real fun) (?:gets?|got|begins?|start(?:s|ed)? to get)\b
positive_examples: Here's where it gets interesting: the second replica had already acked.
This is when things get weird, because the clock went backwards.
negative_examples: Here is where the request enters the proxy tier.
This is where we found the off-by-one, at line 212 of the encoder.
That is when the operator ran the rollback command.
tier2.repair: State the fact without staging it: "the second replica had already acked, so the coordinator counted one ack twice."
tier2.detection_note: Inferred, not in the source. The regex is narrow because the locative "here is where" is genuinely useful in engineering prose ("here is where the request enters the proxy tier") - only the pro-form subjects it/things/the fun are matched, which is what separates suspense-building from location-marking. Zero corpus hits, but the sample of this exact construction in the corpus is also zero, so the separation is untested against real usage.

tier2.name: overfamiliar-address
tier2.regex: \blet'?s (?:dive|unpack|jump in|take a peek|explore together|break (?:this|it) down)\b|\bbuckle up\b|\bstrap in\b|\btrust me[,.:;]|\byou'?re (?:gonna|going to) (?:love|like) (?:this|it)\b|\bstay with me here\b|\bhang tight\b

Let's dive into the scheduler internals.

negative_examples: Let's consider a potential sequence of events with this fallback.
Let's say a service has two APIs, start() and end().
Let's call this value ContainerMemoryProportion.
The Elastic Load Balancing Deep Dive talk covers this at re:Invent 2016.
tier2.repair: Delete the run-up and start at the content: "The scheduler picks the next task by vruntime." For "trust me", supply the measurement instead of the assurance.
tier2.source_quote: Users complained about the model being oddly overfamiliar in conversation, which prompted an investigation into specific verbal tics.
tier2.detection_note: Overfamiliarity is the user-facing symptom the source says triggered the tic investigation, so the register is source-attested even though these specific phrases are not. Critical constraint: "let's" cannot be banned. It appears 13 times correctly in the corpus (AWS "let's consider", "let's say"; KEP-2400 "let's call it TotalPodsSwapAvailable"; Gregg "let's try tsc") in its legitimate first-person-plural-reasoning sense. Only the tour-guide verbs are matched. "Deep dive" is excluded entirely because it appears as a real AWS talk title in the corpus.

tier2.name: decorative-emoji
positive_examples: Shipped the fix 🚀 and latency recovered.
Great work on the migration ✨
negative_examples: | unscheduled Pod | ✅ create | ❌ update |
The p99 rose from 12ms to 400ms after the deploy.
Use → to denote the state transition.
tier2.repair: Delete. If the emoji was carrying status, use a word or a table cell that a grep can find.

The naive version over-fires badly: ✅ and ❌ appear 8 times in KEP-3521's feature-gate compatibility table, which is a real Kubernetes enhancement proposal, and status checkmarks are standard in KEPs and RFCs. tier2.name: magic-as-explanation
positive_examples: The replication layer magically reconciles the divergence.
Some wizardry in the query planner picks the right index.
The secret sauce is in the admission controller.
negative_examples: Distributed systems do not magically become consistent.
The magic number 0xCAFEBABE identifies a class file.
Magic Transit customers could not advertise their prefixes.
The value will not magically appear in the replica.
tier2.repair: Name the algorithm: "the query planner picks the index by comparing estimated rows scanned against the covering-index cost."
tier2.detection_note: Inferred. Two guards carry this rule. First, bare "magic" is unlintable: it appears four times legitimately in the corpus as the Cloudflare product Magic Transit and in Dan Luu's "the magic of LLMs", and "magic number", "magic byte", "magic constant" and MagicMock are core technical vocabulary - so only "it's magic"-style predicative frames are matched. Second, the negated forms are excluded by lookbehind, because "does not magically become consistent" is skeptical engineering prose asserting the opposite of the tell. The negated-form exclusion means an author writing "never magically" or "rarely magically" will still trip it; widen the lookbehind list if that shows up.

tier2.name: persona-noun-inflation
tier2.regex: \btapestry\b|\bin the realm of\b|\ba testament to\b|\brich (?:landscape|tapestry)\b|\bnavigate the (?:complex|intricate|challenging|treacherous)\b|\b(?:10x|rock ?star|ninja|guru|wizard)\s+(?:engineer|developer|programmer|coder|dev)s?\b
positive_examples: The service mesh is a rich tapestry of interacting timeouts.
In the realm of distributed consensus, quorum size matters.
The uptime record is a testament to the on-call rotation.
negative_examples: The retry landscape across our clients is inconsistent; here are the four clients.
We had to navigate a version skew between the agent and the control plane.
This is strong evidence that the on-call rotation is working.
tier2.repair: "In the realm of X" is "in X" or nothing. "A testament to" is "evidence that", which then obliges you to say evidence of what.
tier2.detection_note: Inferred, and not from this source - included because the mechanism predicts that any register-elevating word class the reward favours will saturate. The rule is deliberately tiny. The obvious longer list is unshippable: robust, crucial, pivotal, underscores, landscape and navigate all appear repeatedly and correctly in the corpus (Dynamo on crucial requirements, AWS on robust timeout mechanisms, AWS on what load shedding underscores), and banning them is exactly the over-fire that teaches an author to ignore the linter. Note "ninja" is only matched when it modifies a person noun, because ninja is a build system.

tier2.name: affective-tricolon
positive_examples: The strangeness must be acknowledged, analyzed, and enjoyed.
The result was measured, replicated, and celebrated.
negative_examples: The request is validated, authorized, and logged before it reaches the handler.
Writes are batched, compressed, and flushed every 200ms.
The system must be scalable, available, and durable.
tier2.repair: Cut the third item. "Acknowledged and analyzed" is the actionable pair; the affective closer is decoration and usually is not a thing the reader can do.
tier2.source_quote: The world is complex and strange, and its strangeness must be acknowledged, analyzed, and enjoyed.
tier2.detection_note: The trigger example is the rewarded system prompt itself, which is unusually direct evidence: the persona the reward optimised for was written in this cadence, so the cadence is in the gradient. The rule must not be generalised to tricolons as such - engineering prose is full of correct ones (validated/authorized/logged, scalable/available/durable) - so it fires only when the third member is affective rather than operational. That narrowness means it misses affective tricolons built from non -ed forms.

tier2.name: one-line-closer
positive_examples: That's the real win.
That is the magic: the reader never blocks.
And that's it.
negative_examples: That is the real cost: 3.2 s added to p99.
That is where the request is dropped, between the LB and the pod.
That is the takeaway from the graph above, and here is the number: 14 ms.
tier2.repair: Delete the closer. If it carries a claim the section has not made, replace it with the claim and its number.
tier2.detection_note: Catches the templated closers only. The general form - any short evaluative sentence ending a section - needs a human read, or a heuristic like "final sentence of a section, under 8 words, contains no noun that appears elsewhere in the section". The third negative example shows the failure mode of widening the noun list: "takeaway" followed by evidence is fine.

tier2.name: arguing-with-no-one

The regex fires only on unattributed, unnamed objectors ("some might argue"), not on a stated alternative or an attributed reviewer. Named-source objections must stay.

tier3.repair: Merge the sentences or change the subject: "She traced the spike to a retry storm and filed INC-4471."
tier3.detection_note: Needs sentence segmentation, not a regex: flag three or more consecutive sentences in one paragraph that share their first two tokens. Suppress when the sentences form a parallel data series (each contains a distinct numeral or a distinct metric name) or when they are numbered/bulleted steps - both are deliberate parallelism and appear in the negative examples.
tier3.source_quote: **Repeated sentence openings** | "She noted... She noted... She filed..."

tier3.name: dropped-hyphenated-pairs
positive_examples: the team is cross-functional and solution-oriented
a data-driven, customer-obsessed roadmap
negative_examples: the write-ahead log is copy-on-write and lock-free
end-to-end p99 on the read-modify-write path
a zero-copy, single-threaded, non-blocking reader
tier3.detection_note: DROPPED for technical prose. Hyphenated compounds are the native vocabulary of systems writing (write-ahead, copy-on-write, lock-free, zero-copy, end-to-end, read-modify-write), so both a word list and a density threshold fire on correct documents at rates that would train the author to ignore the linter. The adjectival slop pairs it would catch (cross-functional, data-driven) are better handled by the ai-vocabulary list if they matter.
tier3.source_quote: **Hyphenated pairs everywhere** (*weak alone*) | "the team is cross-functional"

tier3.name: heading-echoed-in-first-sentence
positive_examples: ## Performance\nSpeed matters.
## Rollback\nRollback is important to consider.
negative_examples: ## Retry budget\nThe retry budget is 3 attempts over 250 ms, shared across the hedge.
## Cold start\nCold start costs 4.2 s, of which 3.1 s is class loading.
tier3.repair: Let the heading do the work. Open the section on the first fact the heading does not already carry.
tier3.detection_note: Needs structure, not a regex: for each heading, take its content words and the first sentence of its body, and flag when the sentence adds no content word beyond the heading's. A naive overlap test over-fires on the negative examples, where the first sentence repeats the subject because it is attaching a number to it - so the test must be "adds no new content word", not "repeats the heading". Low confidence as a mechanical check.
tier3.source_quote: **A heading repeated in the first sentence** | "## Performance" + "Speed matters."

tier3.name: dropped-previous-version-narration
positive_examples: This function was added to replace the legacy parser.
This field was renamed from `ttl_ms` in the previous revision of this doc.
negative_examples: Background: v1 used a global lock; this RFC replaces it with per-shard locks.
We reverted to the v2 codec after the incident; v3 remains disabled.
The migration removes the dual-write path added in Q2.
tier3.detection_note: DROPPED for technical prose. Describing what the previous version did is the entire job of an RFC's background section, a postmortem's timeline, and a migration plan, as the negative examples show. The tell only exists in reference and API documentation, where the reader wants current behaviour; if the linter can identify those files (docs/reference, generated API pages) the rule could be re-enabled scoped to them, but corpus-wide it fires on correct writing.
tier3.source_quote: **Writing about the previous version** | "This function was added to replace..."

tier3.name: dropped-false-ranges-and-synonym-cycling
positive_examples: The fix took between four and five days.
The service, the system, the platform - each term for the same daemon.
negative_examples: The rollout took 4-5 days depending on the region.
We call it the router in code and the gateway in the diagram; both names appear in the schema.
tier3.detection_note: DROPPED, and dropped by the source too: version 3.0.0 removed false ranges and synonym cycling because Wikipedia now classes them as human habits. Listed here so the linter's owner knows they were considered and rejected rather than missed. Ranges and elegant variation are both ordinary in engineering prose.
tier3.source_quote: dropped false ranges and synonym cycling, which Wikipedia now lists as human habits or historical

tier3.name: rule-of-three
positive_examples: The platform is fast, flexible, and future-proof.
It offers dependable, value-driven experiences that showcase the state's rich history, spiritual heritage, and natural beauty.
negative_examples: The pipeline reads from Kafka, enriches from the feature store, and writes to Pinot.
The API must be idempotent, retryable, and observable.
tier3.repair: Cut to the one or two members that are load-bearing, or expand each into its own sentence with evidence. A triple of evaluative adjectives is almost always one real claim padded to sound thorough.
tier3.source_quote: LLMs overuse the rule of three . This can take different forms, from "adjective, adjective, adjective" to "short phrase, short phrase, and short phrase". [...] LLMs often use this structure to make superficial analyses appear more comprehensive.
tier3.detection_note: No regex, and I could not construct one that survives contact with engineering prose. The 'X, Y, and Z' shape is how engineers correctly enumerate pipeline stages, dependencies, and invariants; both negative examples are exemplary technical writing in exactly that shape. Even restricting to adjective triples fires on 'idempotent, retryable, and observable'. The distinguishing feature is semantic — are the three members independently checkable facts, or three synonyms for 'good'? — which needs a human or an LLM judge, not a pattern. A weak heuristic a script can run: flag triples where all three members are evaluative adjectives drawn from the puffery lexicon.

tier3.name: elegant-variation-coreference
positive_examples: The service accepts writes. The platform then fans them out. This solution guarantees ordering per key. The system retries on failure.
Yankilevsky faced obstacles in expressing their creativity freely, and the non-conformist artists found a community of like-minded creators.
negative_examples: The ranking service accepts writes. The ranking service fans them out to three shards. The ranking service retries on a 503.
We compared Raft and Paxos; Raft was easier to reason about, and Paxos needed fewer round trips in the steady state.
tier3.repair: Pick one name per referent and repeat it. In engineering prose, repetition of a proper name is a feature: it makes the text greppable and removes the ambiguity of whether 'the platform' and 'the system' are the same thing.
tier3.source_quote: Older AI models may include a repetition penalty, meant to discourage it from reusing words too often. [...] Lexical diversity/elegant variation
tier3.detection_note: No regex. Mechanically approximable but not as a line pattern: within a section, collect generic head nouns from a fixed set (service, platform, system, solution, component, framework, offering, tool) and flag when three or more distinct ones appear with no intervening proper noun binding them, since that is the state where a reader cannot tell how many things are being discussed. Definite-article noun phrases naming DIFFERENT real components (the second negative) must be excluded, which is why this needs a coreference judgement rather than a match. The source also warns that non-native English speakers are taught to vary vocabulary, so this is weak evidence of AI authorship even when it is a real writing defect.
